questions.title: If FlashAttention-2 is already fast, why does it only achieve 35% utilization on the H100 GPU?
questions.question_body: I am reading the FlashAttention-3 paper and it mentions that while FlashAttention-2 was a significant improvement over standard attention, it only achieves about 35% utilization on the Hopper H100 GPU. The authors suggest this is because FlashAttention-2 follows a 'simplified synchronous model.' Can someone explain what 'synchronous' means in the context of GPU kernels? Does it mean the hardware is sitting idle while waiting for memory, or is there something else going on with the instruction scheduling?

questions.title: How does 'Producer-Consumer asynchrony' differ from standard parallel execution in CUDA?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a 'warp-specialized' scheme where warps are split into producers (handling data movement) and consumers (handling computation). In my understanding of GPU programming, threads within a warp usually execute the same instructions in lock-step. How can a single warp be split into producer and consumer roles? Does this mean some threads in the warp are doing TMA loads while others are doing WGMMA instructions simultaneously?

questions.title: Why does the k-major layout constraint specifically affect the $\mathbf{V}$ matrix in FP8 WGMMA?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.3, the authors explain that for FP8 WGMMA, only the k-major format is supported for input operands in shared memory. They mention that this necessitates an in-kernel transpose for the $\mathbf{V}$ matrix. I'm confused about why this is a problem for $\mathbf{V}$ specifically. Since the attention output is $\mathbf{O} = \text{softmax}(\alpha \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top)\mathbf{V}$, doesn't the $\mathbf{V}$ matrix naturally align with the row-wise operations of the softmax? Why does the k-major requirement for the Tensor Cores force us to transpose it?

questions.title: How does the 'pingpong' scheduling avoid stalls between softmax and GEMM operations?
questions.question_body: The paper describes a 'pingpong' scheduling where warpgroup 1 performs softmax while warpgroup 2 performs GEMMs. The authors state that the exponential function (required for softmax) has much lower throughput than matmul operations. Is the goal here to keep the Tensor Cores busy 100% of the time? If warpgroup 1 is doing softmax, is the hardware's Tensor Core unit completely idle, or is it still processing the instructions from warpgroup 2?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind 'Incoherent Processing' for mitigating quantization error?
questions.question_body: The paper suggests multiplying $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ by a random orthogonal matrix $\mathbf{M}$ before quantizing to FP8. Mathematically, I see that $(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{M})(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{M})^	op = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^	op$ because $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{M}^	op = \mathbf{I}$. However, I don't understand the intuition of how this 'spreads out' outliers. If a row in $\mathbf{K}$ has one extremely large value, how does multiplying by a random matrix $\mathbf{M}$ make that value 'easier' to represent in a low-precision format like FP8 (e4m3)?

questions.title: In the 2-stage pipeline, how does the algorithm guarantee correctness if we 'commit but do not wait' for $\mathbf{S}_{next}$?
questions.question_body: In Algorithm 2, the consumer warpgroup computes $\mathbf{S}_{next}$ and 'commits but does not wait' (line 10), then immediately proceeds to compute $\mathbf{O}_i$ using $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{cur}$ (line 12). I am confused about the dependency. If $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_{cur}$ is derived from $\mathbf{S}_{cur}$, and we are moving toward the next iteration, how does the hardware ensure that the calculations for the current $\mathbf{O}_i$ update aren't mixed up with the values from the next iteration? Does the 'register pressure' section imply that we are using specific registers to buffer these intermediate values?
